analysis.one_liner: Requires shareholder approval and public disclosure before public companies spend on political campaigns.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote, after being introduced in 2011 with 13 Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Citizens United decision allowed corporations to spend unlimited money on elections, this bill would have required public companies to tell shareholders how much they plan to spend on politics and win a majority shareholder vote before spending it. It would also require quarterly public reports of every political expenditure, a public board vote on any political spending over $50,000, and disclosure of payments to trade associations that can be passed along to outside political groups. Executives who spent without authorization would be personally liable for triple the amount.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders who own the companies, and voters who want to see which corporations are funding which candidates and causes, including spending routed through trade associations and other intermediaries that today goes undisclosed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shareholders and voters seeking campaign-spending transparency

how_it_helps.text: Before any company spends on elections, a majority of its outstanding shares must vote to authorize the spending, and the proxy materials must describe what the money is for [S2][S3].

Companies must file quarterly reports naming every political expenditure, the candidate supported or opposed, and each director's vote authorizing it, posted publicly and searchable on the SEC's website [S2][S3].
Any board vote on a political expenditure over $50,000 must be made public within 48 hours, closing the gap where corporate money flows to campaigns with no one on record [S2][S3].

Dues paid to trade associations and certain tax-exempt groups — a common channel for corporate political money that reaches outside groups — must be disclosed if they could be used for political spending [S3].

Institutional investors such as pension and mutual funds must disclose how they voted on corporate political-spending authorizations, and are protected from lawsuits for choosing not to invest in politically active companies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their executives, who face compliance costs, quarterly reporting, personal liability for triple any unauthorized political expenditure, and the loss of a low-visibility channel for influencing elections. Trade associations and tax-exempt political intermediaries lose the anonymity of corporate funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies and corporate political intermediaries

drawbacks.text: Requiring approval by a majority of all outstanding shares is a high bar — most shareholders do not vote in routine matters — so the provision could function as a near-prohibition on corporate political spending rather than a disclosure rule [S3].
The bill adds compliance costs for every public company: quarterly SEC reports, board votes and 48-hour public disclosures, and annual summaries of political spending [S2][S3].

Direct lobbying by registered lobbyists and company-run political action committees are carved out, so some of the most common forms of corporate political activity remain outside the shareholder-approval requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — voters and shareholders learning who is bankrolling which candidates, including through trade-association pass-throughs — addresses a real gap left after court decisions allowed unlimited corporate election spending. The costs are real but mainly fall on companies that would otherwise spend without public record. The majority-of-all-shares authorization standard is aggressive and could stop most corporate political spending outright, which supporters would call accountability and critics would call a de facto ban.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2011 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on July 13, 2011 with five original cosponsors: Blumenthal, Lautenberg, Whitehouse, Brown of Ohio, and Feinstein [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
Twelve senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].
The committee never held a hearing or markup and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that fund political campaigns, their executives who make the spending decisions, and the trade associations and outside groups that receive corporate money without disclosure are all better off because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate political spenders and dark-money intermediaries

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as shareholder and public accountability for corporate political spending [S3].

for.name: 12 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican did [S4].

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

against.name: Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never brought the bill to committee action during the two years it was pending before the committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill was never opposed on the floor because it never got there.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations making political expenditures
industries.note: Companies would need shareholder approval, public board votes, and quarterly disclosure for political spending, and executives would owe triple damages for unauthorized spending. The industry's interest in undisclosed political influence runs against voters' interest in knowing who funds campaigns.

The bill targets dues and payments from corporations to these groups when they could be used for election spending, exposing the main channel by which corporate money reaches outside political groups without a public record.

industries.industry: Institutional investment managers (pension and mutual funds)
industries.note: They gain new annual voting-disclosure duties but also a legal safe harbor protecting them from suits for divesting from politically active companies, which supports shareholders' ability to respond to corporate political spending.
